column1: Topic|Track|Meaning|Core concepts|Practice|Failure mode|Evidence

Introduction|01 Role and Glossary|An FDE turns a customer's operational problem into a working, adopted software system while feeding reusable lessons back into the product.|Distinguish product engineering from customer-specific delivery; Own discovery, implementation, deployment, and handover; Work within customer data and security constraints; Measure adoption and business outcomes rather than demo quality|Write a one-page engagement brief for an internal support assistant: users, current workflow, measurable bottleneck, data owners, constraints, and decision makers.|Building a technically impressive demo before confirming that its output changes a real workflow.|Explain the engagement from business pain to operating ownership, including a reason to stop the project.

Roles & Responsabilities|01 Role and Glossary|Responsibilities span technical depth and field ownership; the exact balance depends on the employer and engagement.|Interview operators and sponsors; Audit data and integrations; Design and implement a narrow vertical slice; Deploy, observe, document, and transfer ownership; Distinguish accountability from tasks delegated to platform or security teams|Create a responsibility matrix for discovery, access approval, data quality, release approval, incident response, and training.|Assuming that an impressive prototype transfers responsibility for security or operations to someone else.|Every delivery activity has an accountable owner and an explicit handoff condition.

From X to FDE|01 Role and Glossary|A transition into FDE work builds on existing engineering strengths and closes gaps in customer discovery, AI reliability, and production ownership.|Assess existing full-stack and infrastructure skills; Practice ambiguity reduction; Build customer-facing artifacts; Demonstrate systems thinking and evaluation; Tailor preparation to actual job descriptions|Take one previous project and rewrite it as an FDE case study with stakeholder decisions, deployment constraints, adoption evidence, and lessons returned to product.|Collecting certificates without evidence of delivering under customer constraints.|A portfolio includes a working system, decision log, measured result, and honest failure analysis.

FDE Tiers|01 Role and Glossary|FDE labels and tiers are employer-specific descriptions of technical scope, customer ownership, and product influence, not a universal credential ladder.|Compare implementation-heavy and research-adjacent roles; Identify expected autonomy; Separate seniority from domain specialization; Read hiring rubrics and delivery expectations; Avoid treating compensation reports as stable guarantees|Compare three job descriptions across coding depth, cloud access, travel, model work, enterprise integration, and ownership.|Preparing for a generic FDE title when the actual role requires a different technical profile.|Explain which roles fit your evidence today and the concrete gaps for the next scope of ownership.

Delta|01 Role and Glossary|In this FDE glossary, Delta refers to terminology associated with a field-deployed engineering model; it is not automatically the Delta Lake storage format.|Check the employer-specific meaning; Separate customer problem ownership from deployment tooling; Connect field learning to reusable product improvements; Distinguish role terminology from similarly named technologies|Write a glossary entry contrasting a deployment-team role, a change in a metric, and Delta Lake, and verify the intended meaning with the source or employer.|Assuming that every occurrence of Delta means the same role or data technology.|Resolve the meaning from context and avoid treating one company's terminology as an industry standard.

Last-Mile Integration|01 Role and Glossary|Last-mile integration makes a general product useful inside a customer's actual identities, data, approvals, and day-to-day tools.|Map systems of record; Handle identity and permissions; Translate schemas and business rules; Plan retries and reconciliation; Embed outputs in the existing operator workflow|Connect a support assistant to a ticket sandbox, preserve tenant identity, and require approval before a ticket update.|Finishing the model interaction while leaving authentication, workflow fit, and exception handling unresolved.|A user completes the real task in the target workflow, including error and fallback paths.

Day 2 Operations|01 Role and Glossary|Day 2 begins after launch and covers reliability, maintenance, incidents, access changes, cost, and continuous improvement.|Assign operational owners; Define service objectives; Test backup and restore; Plan dependency and prompt changes; Monitor quality and adoption; Rehearse incidents and rollback|Write and rehearse a runbook for provider outage, bad document ingestion, access revocation, and a quality regression.|Calling a system production-ready because the first deployment succeeded.|Another engineer can detect, diagnose, recover, and communicate an incident using the runbook.

UAT|01 Role and Glossary|User acceptance testing asks whether representative users can complete agreed business tasks safely, not merely whether automated tests pass.|Translate requirements into observable acceptance criteria; Include role-specific workflows; Cover negative and exception cases; Record blockers and sign-off; Separate UAT from model evaluation and security testing|Run five realistic support cases with an operator, a supervisor, and a read-only user; record outcome and required escalation.|Using developer-written happy paths as a substitute for user acceptance.|Business owners sign off on documented workflows, limitations, unresolved defects, and release conditions.

Productized Consulting|01 Role and Glossary|Productized consulting packages repeatable delivery knowledge into bounded offerings without hiding customer-specific uncertainty.|Define a repeatable outcome; Standardize discovery inputs and delivery artifacts; State exclusions and change control; Reuse tested components; Feed repeated needs into a maintained product|Design a fixed-scope data-readiness audit with inputs, outputs, timeline assumptions, acceptance criteria, and an escalation path.|Promising fixed delivery effort while access, source quality, and stakeholder availability remain unknown.|An engagement can be repeated with consistent artifacts while exceptions remain explicit.

Embedded Engineering|01 Role and Glossary|Embedded engineers work closely with customer teams to learn the operational context and deliver changes within it.|Observe actual work; Build trust without bypassing governance; Collaborate with platform and business teams; Maintain product boundaries; Document decisions and reduce dependency on a single engineer|Shadow an operator workflow, map the workarounds, and validate one improvement with the user and system owner.|Becoming the permanent manual integration layer instead of leaving a maintainable system.|The customer can operate the delivered workflow and the product team receives reusable requirements.

Learn a Language|02 Programming and Systems|Language proficiency means being able to build, debug, test, package, and operate a complete service, not only solve syntax exercises.|Choose one primary language; Learn collections and error handling; Understand concurrency and I/O; Use dependency management and tests; Read stack traces and service logs|Build a command-line data audit and a small authenticated API that share validated domain models.|Switching languages repeatedly before being able to ship one complete, tested system.|Implement and troubleshoot an end-to-end feature without relying on generated code you cannot explain.

Python|02 Programming and Systems|Python is a common FDE language for data processing, AI integration, and service development.|Use virtual environments and pinned dependencies; Model inputs explicitly; Handle exceptions and cleanup; Understand iterators, async I/O, and blocking work; Test pure logic separately from service clients|Build an ingestion command that validates records, reports rejected rows, and retries a sandbox API with bounded backoff.|Notebook-only code with hidden state, broad exception handlers, or secrets committed to source control.|A fresh environment can run documented commands, tests, and a sample job with deterministic fixture inputs.

JavaScript / TypeScript|02 Programming and Systems|JavaScript runs browser and server applications; TypeScript adds static contracts but does not validate untrusted runtime data.|Understand promises and the event loop; Use strict types and discriminated unions; Validate API boundaries at runtime; Separate UI state from server state; Handle cancellation and errors|Create a typed ticket API client that validates responses and presents loading, empty, failure, and success states.|Assuming a TypeScript annotation proves an external payload has the expected shape.|Malformed responses fail visibly and safely while valid responses retain useful inferred types.

Java / Scala|02 Programming and Systems|Java and Scala matter when customer platforms, JVM services, or data infrastructure already depend on them.|Understand JVM tooling and dependencies; Learn collections and concurrency; Read Java service contracts; Use Scala where Spark or an existing stack requires it; Integrate through stable API boundaries|Read and extend a small JVM service or Spark job, adding an input check and a regression test.|Introducing a new language into a customer environment without an operational reason.|Explain the build, runtime configuration, failure handling, and integration contract of the changed component.

Go|02 Programming and Systems|Go is useful for deployable services, infrastructure tools, and concurrency-oriented integrations.|Use interfaces conservatively; Propagate context cancellation; Handle errors explicitly; Bound goroutine concurrency; Test HTTP handlers and resource cleanup|Build a concurrent health-audit command with request deadlines and a fixed worker limit.|Launching unbounded goroutines or ignoring cancellation when a customer request ends.|The tool stays within its concurrency budget and terminates predictably under timeouts.

Rust|02 Programming and Systems|Rust provides memory safety and strong ownership guarantees for systems components where those properties justify its complexity.|Understand ownership and borrowing; Use Result and Option; Distinguish sync and async execution; Minimize unsafe code; Choose libraries with clear maintenance and licensing|Implement a validated streaming-file utility and benchmark its memory use on a large fixture.|Choosing Rust for prestige when an existing maintained service already solves the problem.|Justify the language choice and show correct error handling without unexplained unsafe operations.

C++|02 Programming and Systems|C++ is relevant around native libraries, inference runtimes, and performance-sensitive customer systems.|Understand object lifetime and RAII; Distinguish owning and non-owning references; Use build and dependency tooling; Profile before optimizing; Validate native boundaries and sanitizers|Inspect a native inference wrapper and document data ownership, buffer sizes, and error propagation.|Editing native code without understanding memory lifetime or binary compatibility.|Explain the ownership model and validate the relevant boundary with a focused test or sanitizer run.

DSA & System Design|02 Programming and Systems|Data structures support correct local computation; system design allocates work and state across components under realistic constraints.|Practice arrays, maps, stacks, queues, trees, and graphs; Analyze time and space complexity; Define latency and throughput targets; Design caching, queues, and failure isolation; Explain consistency and capacity tradeoffs|Design a ticket-ingestion service, estimate peak load and storage, and implement deduplication with a clear complexity analysis.|Memorizing architecture diagrams without connecting them to customer load, consistency, and failure requirements.|Defend a simple design numerically and identify the first bottleneck and recovery path.

Git & GitHub|02 Programming and Systems|Version control makes implementation history, review, collaboration, and rollback reproducible.|Use small commits and branches; Read diffs and history; Resolve conflicts deliberately; Review pull requests; Protect default branches; Separate source code from secrets and generated artifacts|Deliver a feature through a pull request with tests, a migration note, and a rollback description.|Treating Git as cloud backup and merging changes without reviewing behavior or deployment impact.|Another engineer can review, reproduce, and safely revert the feature.

Linux Skills|02 Programming and Systems|Linux fluency lets an FDE inspect deployed services, permissions, networking, storage, and process behavior.|Navigate files and permissions; Inspect processes and signals; Read logs and environment settings; Diagnose DNS and sockets; Use pipes and shell quoting; Understand service managers and disk limits|Diagnose a sandbox service that fails because of permissions, a missing environment variable, and an unavailable upstream port.|Running privileged commands before understanding the failure or exposing secrets in diagnostic output.|Produce a minimal diagnosis with evidence and recover without weakening access controls.

Frontend Skills|03 Full Stack and Data|Frontend engineering makes system capabilities usable in the customer's actual task flow.|Build semantic accessible interfaces; Model loading and failure states; Validate user input; Handle authentication transitions; Use responsive layouts; Observe client errors and task completion|Build an operator queue with search, filters, record detail, source citations, and a confirmation step before writes.|Measuring success by visual polish while operators cannot complete the workflow or recover from errors.|Users can complete the task with keyboard navigation and clear feedback on network or permission failures.

HTML|03 Full Stack and Data|HTML supplies the semantic structure that browsers and assistive technologies use to interpret a page.|Use headings and landmarks correctly; Associate labels with inputs; Prefer native buttons and forms; Provide meaningful table structure; Avoid div-only interaction patterns|Create an accessible review form and a ticket table with correct headings, labels, validation feedback, and focus behavior.|Replacing native controls with clickable text that has no keyboard or accessibility semantics.|The interface remains understandable without styling and usable with keyboard-only navigation.

CSS|03 Full Stack and Data|CSS controls presentation and responsive layout without changing the underlying meaning of the document.|Understand cascade and specificity; Use flex and grid; Apply responsive constraints; Preserve visible focus and contrast; Avoid overflow from long content; Respect reduced-motion settings|Style an operator dashboard at narrow and wide widths using realistic long names, errors, and empty states.|Testing a layout only with short placeholder text on one desktop viewport.|No important content overlaps or becomes inaccessible at supported viewport sizes and zoom levels.

JavaScript|03 Full Stack and Data|Browser JavaScript coordinates events, state, network requests, and rendering around the user's task.|Understand lexical scope and closures; Use modules and promises; Handle fetch failures explicitly; Prevent stale request updates; Understand DOM event behavior and input validation|Implement search with cancellation and show which query produced the current result.|An older slow request overwrites the result of a newer query.|Out-of-order responses, retries, and user cancellation behave predictably in a small test.

React|03 Full Stack and Data|React expresses interfaces as components that render from state; correctness depends on clear ownership of that state.|Keep rendering pure; Understand props, state, and effects; Use stable list keys; Separate derived state from stored state; Handle forms and asynchronous server state; Test user-visible behavior|Build a ticket review screen with evidence display, correction controls, and disabled duplicate submission.|Using effects to synchronize every derived value or losing user edits when server data refreshes.|Component behavior is explainable under rerenders, request failures, and navigation.

Backend Skills|03 Full Stack and Data|Backend engineering enforces domain rules, persistence, authorization, and reliable integration behind the UI.|Validate inputs; Enforce tenant and object permissions; Manage transactions; Define API contracts; Offload slow work; Apply deadlines and idempotency; Expose useful operational telemetry|Build a ticket-enrichment API and worker with a durable job record and explicit retry states.|Putting all logic in one request handler with no timeout, authorization boundary, or replay protection.|A duplicate request or failed worker cannot silently corrupt state or cross tenant boundaries.

Node.js|03 Full Stack and Data|Node.js provides a JavaScript runtime for I/O-oriented services and integration tooling.|Understand event-loop blocking; Stream large payloads; Propagate errors and cancellation; Manage configuration; Pin dependencies; Use worker execution for CPU-heavy tasks|Build a streaming CSV validation endpoint and compare memory consumption against loading the whole file.|Performing CPU-heavy work or unbounded buffering on the request event loop.|Concurrent requests remain responsive while large or malformed uploads are rejected safely.

SQL|03 Full Stack and Data|SQL retrieves and transforms relational data while preserving an explicit understanding of row grain and joins.|Use joins, grouping, and window functions; Understand NULL and three-valued logic; Parameterize queries; Read query plans; Use transactions; Test duplicate and missing-key cases|Calculate ticket resolution time per team and prove that joining event history does not double-count tickets.|A join multiplies rows and makes the business metric look better or worse than reality.|Reconcile query output with a hand-checked sample and explain the query plan for realistic data volume.

PostgreSQL|03 Full Stack and Data|PostgreSQL is a transactional relational database with strong constraints, indexing, and useful extension capabilities.|Model primary and foreign keys; Use transactions and isolation deliberately; Index measured access paths; Inspect EXPLAIN ANALYZE; Plan migrations and backups; Enforce tenant access consistently|Create tickets, events, and review decisions with constraints; test a migration and restore a backup into a separate database.|Using application validation alone to enforce invariants or assuming a backup guarantees a working restore.|Demonstrate concurrency correctness, query performance, and a documented restore procedure.

NoSQL DBs|03 Full Stack and Data|NoSQL describes multiple data models whose tradeoffs differ; document, key-value, graph, and wide-column stores are not interchangeable.|Choose from access patterns; Understand partition keys and hot partitions; Design consistency and expiry; Denormalize with a reconciliation plan; Distinguish caches from systems of record|Compare a relational ticket record, a document snapshot, and a Redis cache entry, including invalidation and failure behavior.|Selecting a store because it scales in theory while ignoring required joins or transactional updates.|Explain exactly which queries and consistency guarantees justify the chosen store.

APIs Design|03 Full Stack and Data|API design creates stable contracts for data and actions across teams and systems.|Name resources and operations clearly; Define schemas and errors; Use pagination and versioning; Apply idempotency to retryable writes; Enforce authorization; Document rate limits and deadlines|Write an OpenAPI contract for creating an enrichment job and polling its state, including duplicate submission and validation errors.|Treating a successful HTTP response as proof that the business operation completed.|Clients can distinguish accepted work, completed work, retryable failure, and permanent rejection.

GraphQL|03 Full Stack and Data|GraphQL lets clients request typed fields through a schema, while resolvers still own authorization, efficiency, and domain behavior.|Understand schema, queries, and mutations; Avoid N+1 resolver calls; Bound query depth and complexity; Apply object authorization; Plan pagination and schema evolution|Expose tickets with paginated events and prove a user cannot access another tenant through nested fields.|Assuming schema types enforce permission checks or prevent expensive queries.|A nested query has bounded cost and the same authorization guarantees as direct API access.

Data Engineering Skills|03 Full Stack and Data|Data engineering turns customer source data into trustworthy, traceable inputs for applications and analytics.|Audit sources and ownership; Define schemas and grain; Build incremental loads; Track lineage and freshness; Quarantine bad records; Make jobs replayable and observable|Create a source-to-serving data contract for tickets and documents with quality checks and an owner for each field.|Starting model work before discovering that identifiers, timestamps, or permissions are unreliable.|A sampled output can be traced to its source and regenerated after a controlled backfill.

Data Modeling|03 Full Stack and Data|Data modeling makes business entities, relationships, identifiers, and historical changes explicit.|Distinguish conceptual, logical, and physical models; Define entity grain; Map keys and cardinality; Choose normalization or denormalization deliberately; Represent slowly changing attributes and deletions|Draw a model for customers, users, tickets, documents, and entitlements, including one-to-many relationships and retention rules.|Mixing current state and event history in a table without a clear time interpretation.|Two engineers derive the same metric and authorization result from the documented model.

Data Pipelines|03 Full Stack and Data|A pipeline moves and transforms data through controlled stages with visible correctness and recovery behavior.|Distinguish batch and streaming; Implement checkpoints and watermarks; Handle late and duplicate data; Validate schema contracts; Plan backfills and dead-letter handling; Measure freshness|Ingest ticket updates incrementally, deliberately replay a batch, and reconcile the output against source counts.|Assuming exactly-once processing without examining external writes, offsets, and failure boundaries.|A restart or replay produces the documented result without unexplained loss or duplication.

Data Warehouses|03 Full Stack and Data|A warehouse supports analytical workloads and governed metrics, usually with different access and performance patterns from an operational database.|Understand facts and dimensions; Define shared business metrics; Manage incremental transformations; Partition and cluster appropriately; Track lineage and query cost; Preserve historical meaning|Build a small ticket-performance mart with a documented metric definition and data freshness indicator.|Using a warehouse aggregate as a live transactional truth or creating inconsistent metric definitions.|A business metric reconciles with source samples and its refresh delay and caveats are visible.

Spark|03 Full Stack and Data|Spark distributes data processing when workload size and computation justify cluster coordination costs.|Understand lazy execution; Inspect partitions and shuffles; Prefer built-in transformations; Handle skew and joins; Use appropriate file formats; Profile before increasing cluster size|Process a partitioned event dataset and compare a skewed join with a revised partitioning strategy.|Using a cluster for a small local task or hiding expensive shuffles behind concise code.|Explain the execution plan, data movement, and cost of a representative job.

Airflow|03 Full Stack and Data|Airflow orchestrates scheduled workflows and dependencies; it is not itself the engine for all data processing.|Design idempotent tasks; Understand scheduling and data intervals; Separate retries from backfills; Use connections and secret management; Keep large data out of task metadata; Alert on missed outcomes|Create an ingestion, validation, and publish DAG; rerun a failed interval without duplicating published records.|Tasks depend on current wall-clock state and cannot correctly backfill a historical interval.|A failed task can be retried and a past interval can be reproduced with documented inputs.

AI Engineering Skills|04 AI Engineering|AI engineering combines model behavior with deterministic software, evaluation, data controls, and production delivery.|Start from a task and baseline; Select models through measured tests; Add retrieval or tools only when needed; Version prompts and datasets; Control output schemas, cost, and latency; Design fallback paths|Ship a support-answer prototype with citations, abstention, a small evaluation set, and a documented model choice.|Optimizing a prompt on memorable examples without a held-out test set.|A repeatable evaluation shows improvement over a simple baseline within an agreed operational budget.

LLM Fundamentals|04 AI Engineering|A language model produces token distributions conditioned on supplied context; fluent output is not a guarantee of factual correctness.|Distinguish training from inference; Understand tokenization and context limits; Separate model weights from supplied knowledge; Know sampling and structured-output constraints; Measure hallucination, latency, and token cost|Compare three tasks: extracting a date, answering from a document, and answering without evidence; record when the system should abstain.|Treating a confident answer as verified knowledge or assuming all providers use prompts for training.|Explain why a response was accepted or rejected using evidence, validation, and the provider's actual data policy.

Prompt Engineering|04 AI Engineering|Prompt engineering specifies a task, constraints, examples, and output expectations so that model behavior can be tested.|Separate instructions from untrusted data; Specify an output schema; Use representative examples; State abstention and escalation rules; Version prompt changes; Compare on held-out cases|Create an extraction prompt with a JSON schema and evaluate it on missing, conflicting, and adversarial inputs.|Adding more instructions after each anecdotal failure until the prompt becomes contradictory.|A prompt revision improves measured outcomes without breaking existing cases or weakening boundaries.

Context Engineering|04 AI Engineering|Context engineering chooses the information, tools, memory, and state supplied at each model invocation.|Budget tokens by information value; Retrieve permission-filtered evidence; Isolate untrusted content; Summarize or compact deliberately; Preserve task state outside the prompt; Measure retrieval and context failures separately|Construct an evidence packet with source IDs, timestamps, entitlements, and a strict size budget; test conflicting and stale documents.|Filling the context window indiscriminately or summarizing away a critical constraint.|Explain why every included item is relevant, authorized, current enough, and worth its token cost.

RAGs|04 AI Engineering|Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves external evidence at inference time, then asks a model to answer within that evidence.|Separate ingestion and query pipelines; Chunk by document structure; Version embeddings and indexes; Combine lexical and vector retrieval when useful; Rerank and cite sources; Evaluate retrieval and generation independently|Index a permission-tagged document set, test retrieval recall, and measure supported-answer accuracy with explicit abstention cases.|Retrieving relevant but unauthorized or outdated material and treating citations as proof of correctness.|Answers cite passages that support their claims, and unauthorized documents never enter the model context.

Vector DBs|04 AI Engineering|A vector database indexes embeddings for approximate similarity search and often supports metadata filtering and hybrid retrieval.|Match embedding model and dimensions; Choose distance metrics; Understand approximate recall tradeoffs; Apply tenant filters before returning evidence; Plan deletion and re-embedding; Evaluate against lexical baselines|Build a searchable policy corpus and compare top-k recall for vector-only and hybrid retrieval on a labeled query set.|Changing embedding models without rebuilding vectors or assuming similarity equals factual support.|Measure recall, latency, freshness, deletion behavior, and tenant isolation under representative queries.

Choosing Model Providers|04 AI Engineering|Model choice balances task quality with latency, cost, availability, data policy, geography, and operational support.|Create a task-specific benchmark; Compare context and tool capabilities; Verify data retention and training terms; Check regions and rate limits; Evaluate total workflow cost; Plan model-version changes|Score two providers and one alternative architecture against the same fixtures, including outage and rate-limit behavior.|Choosing from leaderboard rank or token price alone, or silently switching models with different behavior.|A decision record contains measured task results, policy checks, a cost model, and a tested fallback policy.

Prompt Management|04 AI Engineering|Prompt management treats prompts and their dependencies as deployable, testable configuration with traceable versions.|Version prompt templates and variables; Pin model and tool schema dependencies; Track evaluation datasets; Review changes; Use staged rollout and rollback; Record the prompt version with each trace|Release two prompt versions against the same dataset and roll back a deliberately regressed version.|Editing a production prompt directly without an evaluation result or a way to identify affected requests.|Reproduce which prompt, model, retrieval configuration, and tool schema generated a given output.

AI Agents|05 Agents and Coding Tools|An agent uses model-directed decisions and tool results to pursue a goal across multiple steps.|Distinguish deterministic workflows from autonomous decisions; Define allowed tools and authority; Maintain explicit state; Bound iterations, cost, and time; Require approval for consequential actions; Evaluate whole-task success|Build a read-only ticket investigation agent with a maximum step count and a documented human escalation path.|Giving an open-ended agent broad credentials and assuming natural-language instructions enforce permission.|The agent stops safely, reports uncertainty, and cannot perform an action outside server-enforced authority.

Agent Architectures|05 Agents and Coding Tools|An architecture defines where model decisions occur and where deterministic control, state, and verification remain.|Compare chaining, routing, parallel workers, and evaluator loops; Start with a single model call; Introduce autonomy only for measured need; Make transitions explicit; Budget cumulative error and latency|Implement the same support triage task as rules, a fixed LLM workflow, and a bounded agent; compare outcome, cost, and debuggability.|Selecting a multi-agent framework before identifying a task that benefits from dynamic decisions.|Choose the simplest architecture that meets the measured requirements and explain why alternatives lose.

Tools & Functions|05 Agents and Coding Tools|Tool calling lets a model propose structured actions; trusted application code validates and executes them.|Write precise tool schemas and descriptions; Validate arguments; Enforce identity and object permissions; Separate reads from writes; Apply idempotency and deadlines; Return compact structured observations|Expose read_ticket and propose_update tools, with an independently enforced approval step for actual updates.|Assuming the model executes a function itself or trusting tool arguments because they match JSON syntax.|Malformed, unauthorized, repeated, and excessive calls are rejected before any side effect.

Memory & State|05 Agents and Coding Tools|State records the current workflow; memory preserves selected information across steps or sessions, subject to retention and access rules.|Separate ephemeral context from durable state; Use explicit checkpoints; Version state schemas; Scope memory by user and tenant; Support correction and deletion; Treat retrieved memory as untrusted data|Resume an interrupted investigation from a checkpoint while ensuring a different tenant cannot retrieve its history.|Storing unlimited conversation text as permanent truth or repeating an already committed action after restart.|A restart resumes predictably, sensitive memory can be deleted, and side effects are not duplicated.

MCP|05 Agents and Coding Tools|Model Context Protocol standardizes how AI applications connect to tools, resources, and prompts; it does not replace application authorization.|Understand host, client, and server roles; Distinguish tools, resources, and prompts; Negotiate supported capabilities; Use current transport and authentication guidance; Validate server identity and scopes; Treat tool output as untrusted|Expose a read-only ticket lookup through an MCP server and document each permission, transport assumption, and trust boundary.|Treating protocol compatibility as proof that a server, tool, or returned instruction is trustworthy.|A client discovers capabilities and uses only authorized operations with bounded, auditable behavior.

Multi-Agents|05 Agents and Coding Tools|Multiple agents divide work or perspectives, but coordination adds latency, cost, and opportunities for inconsistent state.|Define roles and message contracts; Prefer independent tasks; Centralize shared-state authority; Bound delegation depth; Evaluate coordination overhead; Use a single-agent baseline|Compare a single investigator against separate retrieval and policy-review workers on the same cases.|Adding agents to compensate for an unclear task or letting agents approve one another's sensitive writes.|A measured improvement justifies coordination cost and responsibility for final decisions remains explicit.

Vibe Coding|05 Agents and Coding Tools|AI-assisted coding accelerates implementation only when a human retains control of requirements, verification, security, and maintainability.|Give bounded tasks and relevant context; Inspect diffs; Run tests and type checks; Validate generated dependencies; Review authorization and secrets; Keep deployment approval outside model discretion|Use an assistant to implement one small feature, then explain every changed line and demonstrate a regression test.|Accepting code because it runs once, without understanding data access or failure behavior.|The generated feature meets a written acceptance criterion and passes the same review gates as human-written code.

Claude Code|05 Agents and Coding Tools|Claude Code is an agentic development tool whose usefulness depends on repository context, permissions, and verification discipline.|Consult current vendor documentation; Provide scoped tasks and repository guidance; Review shell and file permissions; Protect credentials; Inspect diffs and tests; Track model and tool configuration|Use a sandbox repository to fix a small defect, capture its test before and after, and inspect every command and file change.|Granting broad terminal or network authority for an underspecified task.|You can reconstruct the task, permissions, changes, validation, and remaining risk from the session evidence.

Codex|05 Agents and Coding Tools|Codex development tooling can assist with code tasks, but its execution mode and permissions must be verified in current documentation.|Distinguish chat, CLI, IDE, and hosted workflows; Check sandbox and approval controls; Supply reproducible tests; Review changes; Verify data handling; Keep production credentials out of the workspace|Run a small fixture-based code task with restricted access and compare the result with the requested acceptance behavior.|Assuming all products using the same model or brand share identical data and execution policies.|The chosen mode has documented permissions, reproducible output, and independently checked changes.

Gemini|05 Agents and Coding Tools|Gemini names a model and product family; API use, chat use, and coding tools have different interfaces and governance settings.|Identify the exact product and model; Check API schemas and quotas; Protect API keys; Verify organization data controls; Evaluate tool and structured-output behavior; Record version assumptions|Compare a schema-constrained extraction task with an existing provider using the same inputs and validation.|Treating a consumer chat feature as equivalent to an enterprise API contract.|Document the exact endpoint, model, account policy, limits, cost, and measured task results.

Cursor|05 Agents and Coding Tools|Cursor is an AI-enabled development environment; editor convenience does not remove the need for repository and credential boundaries.|Review indexing and privacy settings; Supply focused context; Inspect agent permissions; Validate edits with tests; Avoid including secrets; Keep project guidance consistent|Use the editor to implement a UI state fix and inspect the diff, network assumptions, and behavior at narrow widths.|Letting automatic context collection include confidential files that are unrelated to the task.|The feature is verified and the organization's rules for indexed or transmitted code are respected.

OpenClaw|05 Agents and Coding Tools|OpenClaw appears in the live roadmap as an agent tool topic; evaluate the specific current project and deployment rather than inferring safety from its name.|Verify the official source and version; Review available integrations; Isolate runtime credentials; Restrict filesystem and network access; Inspect extension trust; Define audit and shutdown controls|Assess a sandbox installation plan and list each permission, integration, data destination, and recovery action before enabling it.|Installing a rapidly changing agent tool with broad personal or enterprise permissions by default.|A documented threat model and bounded pilot justify every permission and provide a clear kill switch.

OpenCode|05 Agents and Coding Tools|OpenCode is listed as a coding-agent tool; its actual provider configuration, capabilities, and privacy depend on the selected version and setup.|Verify official docs and releases; Configure providers explicitly; Review command approval; Limit workspace access; Inspect plugins and dependencies; Validate generated changes independently|Compare a bounded bug-fix task against another tool using identical tests and a clean sandbox.|Equating open-source availability with a complete security review or with local-only model processing.|Document which code and prompts leave the machine and which commands the tool can execute.

Integration Engineering|06 Integration Cloud and DevOps|Integration engineering connects business systems while preserving contracts, identity, correctness, and recoverability.|Map source and target ownership; Version schemas; Choose APIs, events, or batch appropriately; Handle partial failure; Reconcile state; Apply least privilege and end-to-end tracing|Build an adapter between a ticket sandbox and an enrichment service, including a dead-letter path and replay command.|Assuming both systems commit atomically or retrying side effects without a stable idempotency key.|After an induced failure, both systems reconcile to the documented business state.

Working with Legacy Systems|06 Integration Cloud and DevOps|Legacy integration starts by understanding existing behavior and constraints before changing a system people already depend on.|Map interfaces and undocumented dependencies; Add characterization tests; Prefer adapters and incremental replacement; Protect compatibility; Plan rollback and data reconciliation; Respect maintenance windows|Wrap one legacy export behind a validated adapter and compare results with the current workflow before any cutover.|Rewriting a critical system before learning the exceptions that keep the business running.|A parallel run demonstrates equivalence or documented improvements with a reversible rollout.

Cloud Platforms|06 Integration Cloud and DevOps|Cloud proficiency means operating compute, storage, networking, identity, and managed services as a coherent deployment.|Choose one platform deeply; Design network and identity boundaries; Use managed services deliberately; Understand regions and quotas; Track cost and egress; Plan recovery and ownership|Draw and deploy a sandbox architecture with private data storage, a service identity, monitored compute, and a budget alert.|Choosing services from a catalog without a clear data path, ownership model, or recovery objective.|Explain every trust boundary, recurring cost, and expected failure response in the deployment.

AWS|06 Integration Cloud and DevOps|AWS offers cloud infrastructure and managed services; an FDE should select a small coherent set based on customer constraints.|Understand IAM roles and policies; Use VPC networking; Match compute and storage to access patterns; Protect secrets with managed facilities; Enable logs and budgets; Test restore and least privilege|Deploy a small service using temporary workload identity and private object storage in a sandbox account.|Using long-lived administrator keys or exposing a storage bucket to simplify a demo.|The workload can access only the required resources, and cost and recovery controls are demonstrated.

GCP|06 Integration Cloud and DevOps|Google Cloud deployment combines resource organization, IAM, networking, managed compute, and data services.|Understand projects and service accounts; Use workload identity where appropriate; Scope IAM; Separate application and data access; Monitor quotas and billing; Check regional availability|Deploy an authenticated service with a dedicated identity and access to only one required data resource.|Reusing a broad project-level service account across unrelated workloads.|Permissions, regional assumptions, telemetry, and monthly cost estimates are explicit and testable.

Azure|06 Integration Cloud and DevOps|Azure deployment relies on clear subscription boundaries, Microsoft Entra identity, resource permissions, and network design.|Understand tenants and subscriptions; Prefer managed identities; Use role-based access control; Separate secrets and configuration; Monitor resources and budgets; Check regional and enterprise policy restrictions|Deploy a sandbox service with managed identity and an explicitly scoped storage permission.|Confusing an authenticated Entra principal with authorization to every downstream resource.|A user and workload each receive only their required permissions and access revocation is tested.
